title: Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care
description: SKOS concept scheme of terms and abbreviations defined in the WHO Digital Transformation Handbook for Primary Health Care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems (2024, ISBN 978-92-4-009336-2), cross-linked to the WHO/ITU DPI-H Reference Architecture (smart-ra: dpi-h-ra and full-stac schemes) and the WHO SMART Guidelines DAK vocabulary (smart-base). Acronyms (owner, 2026-10-31): every acronym the handbook uses in its abbreviations table and chapters is a term here with the acronym as notation and a source pointing to its L1 section (litlfred/folio-assistant-core#412).

terms.definition: In the context of person-centred health services, person-centred refers to prioritizing the comprehensive needs of individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the centre of health systems. It involves actively engaging and empowering individuals to have a more active role in their own health and health-care decisions. It shifts the focus of health services away from specific diseases or interventions, towards holistic needs of individuals across the continuum of care and life course (21).

terms.definition: Person-centred point of service system (PCPOSS) are digital systems that facilitate the provision and delivery of health services to individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the point of service or point of care. This includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable health workers to access, record and update individuals’ health information. PCPOSS also includes software capabilities and embedded health interoperability standards that enable screening, managing, treating, and/or communicating with, individuals. PCPOSS encompass various services and application types, including community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical (or health) record systems and personal health records (3).

terms.definition: Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23).
